When a system abuses a citizen, the bureaucracy debates the paperwork. Using policy excuses to hide raw misconduct is the ultimate institutional shield.

Henry Nowak Police Abuse Inquiry
Evidence: equal protection, systemic abuse, accountability

The claim is that police anti-racism policies and procedures are designed to ensure fair, unbiased, and humane treatment for all members of the community.
Stated Judgement: (+1.0, +1.0) — Greater Good

In reality, the appalling treatment of Henry Nowak reveals systemic negligence, with subsequent policy debates acting as a distraction from core police misconduct.
Resulting Judgement: (-1.0, -1.0) — Greater Evil

Verdict: FAIL — The Path of Deception.
Debating whether anti-racism rules caused abuse allows the institution to deflect from its basic failure to protect human dignity.
A Guardian explainer examines whether anti-racism policies led to the mistreatment of Henry Nowak, sorting through institutional claims versus the reality of police behavior.

The Bright Side:
Public scrutiny and detailed journalism keep the focus on police misconduct, preventing the incident from being quietly buried under administrative files.

The Breakdown & Plane Error:
They debate this as a conflict of policy rules and guidelines (HOW). Structurally, it is a Will (WHO) failure: the absence of empathy and basic human care in the action chain.

The Trajectory: The Path of Deception.
When administrative excuses are used to justify or explain away direct physical mistreatment of a citizen...
...it plots a trajectory toward Greater Evil. Intersecting u=-1.0 and psi=-1.0, the system protects itself from liability while leaving citizens exposed to state abuse.

The Unavoidable Truth: No amount of policy jargon can justify the physical mistreatment of a person under police custody.

The Unavoidable Lie: That bad policing is caused by having rules against racism.
